items.prose: A broker claims its new venue gives lower slippage than the old one. The old venue’s long-run mean is 1.8 bp per order. You will test the claim on a sample of orders.
items.question: Which pair of hypotheses fits the claim?

options.why: You put the claim in the null. The null is “no change”, $\mu = 1.8$.
That alternative says slippage rose. The claim is that it fell.
You wrote the hypotheses about the sample mean. They are about the true mean $\mu$.

feedback.correct: No change is the null; lower slippage is the alternative.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The null is no change; the alternative is the claim.

explain.text: The dull story is that the venue changed nothing: $\mu = 1.8$. The claim names a direction, lower, so $H_1: \mu < 1.8$. The sample mean $\bar x$ is the evidence, not a hypothesis.

items.prose: A desk’s trade size has long averaged 500 shares, with known sd 300 shares. This month 225 trades averaged 540 shares. Test $H_0: \mu = 500$.
items.question: What is $z$?

byKey.sigma: You divided by $\sigma$, the spread of one trade. Divide by the standard error, $300/15 = 20$.
byKey.over-n: You divided by $\sigma/n$. The standard error is $\sigma/\sqrt n$.

explain.text: The standard error is $300/\sqrt{225} = 20$ shares. So 540 shares is $z = 40/20 = 2.0$ standard errors above the null mean. That is past 1.96.

items.prose: The trade-size test gave $z = 2.0$, two-sided. You are told $\Phi(2.0) = 0.9772$.
items.question: What is the p-value?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Double the tail beyond $|z| = 2$.

byKey.one-tail: That is one tail. The test is two-sided, so double it.
byKey.phi: That is the area below 2.0. The p-value is in the tails.

explain.text: One tail beyond 2.0 holds $1 - 0.9772 = 0.0228$, so two tails hold 0.0456. That is below 0.05, so we reject $H_0$ at 5%. Luck alone gives a $z$ this far out about one time in 22.

items.prose: A test of $H_0$: “the signal has no edge” gives $p = 0.20$. A colleague concludes: “So the signal has no edge, with 80% confidence.”
items.question: What is the right reading?

options.text: Data like these would be common with no edge, so there is no evidence of an edge
The colleague is right: $1 - p$ is the confidence in $H_0$
options.why: You read $1 - p$ as a chance for a hypothesis. A p-value assumes $H_0$; it gives no chance of $H_0$ or $H_1$.

options.text: There is a 20% chance the signal has an edge
options.why: You read $p$ as a chance of $H_1$. It is a chance about data, assuming $H_0$.

options.text: The test has proved the signal has no edge
options.why: You read “fail to reject” as proof. A small edge could easily produce the same data.

feedback.correct: No evidence of an edge, and no proof of none.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read $p$ as $P(\text{data this extreme} \mid H_0)$.

explain.text: With no edge, data at least this extreme turn up 20% of the time, so they are unremarkable. That is no evidence of an edge. It is not evidence for “no edge” either.

items.prose: A new fund’s 6 monthly returns have mean 2.0% and sample sd 2.5%. The two-sided 5% cut-off for 5 degrees of freedom is 2.571.
items.question: What does the $t$ test of $H_0: \mu = 0$ conclude at 5%?

options.why: You used the normal cut-off. With $s$ from 6 months, the cut-off is 2.571.
You divided by $s$. The standard error is $2.5/\sqrt 6 = 1.02$.

options.text: Fail to reject: the cut-off for 6 degrees of freedom is 2.447
options.why: Right decision, wrong degrees of freedom: $n - 1 = 5$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $t = 2.0/(2.5/\sqrt 6)$ and compare it with 2.571.

explain.text: The standard error is $2.5/\sqrt 6 \approx 1.021\%$, so $t \approx 1.96$. Against the 5-df cut-off of 2.571 that is not enough; the p-value is 0.107. The same 1.96 with $\sigma$ known would sit right on the line.

items.prose: Under $H_0: p = 0.5$, a trader’s wins in 20 trades have $P(W \ge 15) = 0.0207$. A trader won 15. The risk manager tests $H_1: p \ne 0.5$.
items.question: What is the chance, under $H_0$, of a result at least as extreme as 15 wins?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count both tails: 15 or more wins, and 5 or fewer.

byKey.one-tail: That is the top tail. Under $p \ne 0.5$, 5 wins or fewer is just as extreme.
byKey.inside: That is the chance of landing between 6 and 14 wins.

explain.text: Fifteen wins is five above 10, and so is 5 wins. By symmetry each tail holds 0.0207, so the two-sided chance is 0.0414. That is below 0.05.

items.prose: A strategy reports an annualised Sharpe ratio of 1.5 over 3 years of independent returns.
items.question: About what is its $t$ statistic? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the Sharpe ratio by $\sqrt T$, with $T$ in years.

byKey.times-t: You multiplied by $T$. The evidence grows with $\sqrt T$.
byKey.over-root: You divided by $\sqrt T$. More years mean more evidence, so multiply.

explain.text: A Sharpe ratio is mean over sd, so $t = \mathrm{SR}\sqrt T = 1.5\sqrt 3 \approx 2.60$. That clears 1.96. It says nothing yet about how many strategies were tried first.

items.prose: An order router filled 60% of orders. After a change, 2,500 orders fill at 62%. Test $H_0: f = 0.60$ against $H_1: f > 0.60$. You are told $\Phi(2.041) = 0.9794$.
items.question: What is the p-value?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $z$ with the standard error $\sqrt{0.6 \times 0.4/2500}$, then take the upper tail.

byKey.two: You doubled the tail. This alternative is one-sided.
byKey.phi: That is the area below $z$. The p-value is the tail above.

explain.text: The standard error is $\sqrt{0.24/2500} \approx 0.0098$, so $z = 0.02/0.0098 \approx 2.041$. The one-sided p-value is $1 - 0.9794 = 0.0206$. A smaller rise than before is clearer evidence, because 2,500 orders shrink the noise.

items.prose: A strategy truly earns 0.1% a day, with known daily sd 1.5%. You plan a one-sided $z$ test at 5%, whose cut-off is 1.645.
items.question: How many days until an average equal to the true edge gives $z = 1.645$? Round up to a whole day.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $0.1\sqrt n/1.5 = 1.645$ for $n$.

byKey.no-square: That is $\sqrt n$. Square it to get $n$.
byKey.two-sided: You used 1.96, the two-sided cut-off. This test is one-sided.

explain.text: $z = \mu\sqrt n/\sigma$, so $z = 1.645$ needs $\sqrt n = 1.645 \times 1.5/0.1 = 24.675$. Squaring gives $n \approx 608.9$, so 609 days. That is about two and a half years of trading.
